findings.title: Raw recovery codes persisted to user storage
findings.body: createRecoveryCodesCredential serializes the raw (unhashed) generated recovery codes to JSON and passes them as the value of a UserCredentialModel to user.credentialManager().updateCredential(...). The local DB branch goes through RecoveryAuthnCodesCredentialProvider.createCredential(credentialModel) which is responsible for hashing the codes before persistence, but the user-storage branch hands the plaintext list to the user storage. Any user storage provider that does not independently hash the codes (such as the test provider introduced in this PR, which stores input.getChallengeResponse() verbatim in credentialData) will keep recovery codes in plaintext, and the credential 'value' field is left empty while 'credentialData' is misused as the secret store. Recovery codes must never be persisted in plaintext; the helper must hash them before calling updateCredential, exactly as the credential provider does on the local DB path.

findings.title: Used recovery code is not invalidated and not removed after exhaustion
findings.body: In the new RecoveryAuthnCodesCredentialModel.TYPE branch of isValid, the implementation only returns generatedKeys.stream().anyMatch(key -> key.equals(input.getChallengeResponse())). It never marks the consumed code as used, never rewrites the stored credential, and never triggers the credentialModel.allCodesUsed() transition that RecoveryAuthnCodesFormAuthenticator.action relies on. As a result, (a) the same recovery code can be reused on subsequent logins, (b) once all codes have been consumed the credential is never removed and the CONFIGURE_RECOVERY_AUTHN_CODES required action is never added, leaving the user with an apparently infinite pool of one-time codes. The local DB RecoveryAuthnCodesCredentialProvider must therefore be performing this invalidation internally; the user storage provider needs to mirror that behaviour, otherwise the semantics diverge silently between local and federated storage.

findings.title: New getCredentials does not null-check the user lookup
findings.body: getCredentials calls getMyUser(user) and then immediately dereferences myUser.recoveryCodes and myUser.otp without checking for null. Every other method in this class that uses getMyUser (isConfiguredFor, isValid) explicitly checks `if (myUser == null) return false;` first. The new method should follow the same pattern, otherwise a user that is not in the backing map (e.g. an externally-removed user whose adapter is still being inspected) will trigger an NPE deep in the credential lookup.

findings.title: testRecoveryKeysSetupAndLogin does not assert one-time-use semantics
findings.body: The new test only exercises a single successful login with one recovery code and then logs out. It never re-enters with the same code to verify it is rejected, never iterates through all codes to verify the credential is removed and CONFIGURE_RECOVERY_AUTHN_CODES is added, and never verifies the codes are stored hashed. Given that the helper change introduces a plaintext-storage path and the test provider does not invalidate consumed codes, this gap means those regressions would slip through CI.

findings.title: Hardcoded provider ID instead of constant
findings.body: The provider id 'keycloak-recovery-authn-codes' is hardcoded as a string literal in createRecoveryCodesCredential. The companion class RecoveryAuthnCodesCredentialProviderFactory exposes PROVIDER_ID for exactly this purpose; using the constant avoids silent breakage if the provider id is ever renamed.

findings.title: Constructor dereferences Optional without isPresent check
findings.body: RecoveryAuthnCodeInputLoginBean now reads the credential via RecoveryAuthnCodesUtils.getCredential(user) and immediately calls credentialModelOpt.get() to feed RecoveryAuthnCodesCredentialModel.createFromCredentialModel(...). If the credential is missing (e.g. the user has no recovery codes configured, or the credential was just removed because allCodesUsed() was true), this throws NoSuchElementException and the login form rendering fails. The original implementation only read from local storage and would NoSuch on the same condition, but the new code path makes the failure reachable in more scenarios (e.g. federated user whose credential expired). The bean should guard the missing-credential case.
